title: Aggregate productivity: Task speedups shrink during scaling
desc: Shows projections depend on adoption, verification and difficult residual tasks, while reallocation can preserve employment.

kps.k: The central dispute concerns how task-level AI gains translate into aggregate productivity, employment and welfare—not whether AI can accelerate selected tasks.
kps.d: The task-based accounts distinguish technical exposure, profitable adoption, actual use and realised outcomes. Acemoglu links aggregate gains to the economic share of affected tasks and their cost savings; other analyses add capital investment, task reallocation, demand responses and new work. Exposure studies such as GPTs are GPTs measure potential, while platform logs describe interactions rather than job replacement. These distinctions make apparently conflicting estimates partly differences in scope, assumptions and measurement.

qs.q: I show that when AI’s microeconomic effects are driven by cost savings (equiva- lently, productivity improvements) at the task level—due to either automation or task complementarities—its macroeconomic consequences will be given by a version of Hulten’s theorem: GDP and aggregate productivity gains can be estimated by what fraction of tasks are impacted and average task-level cost savings.
qs.a: The Simple Macroeconomics of AI · Academia · 2024

qs.q: This paper’s primary contributions are to provide a set of measurements of LLM impact potential and to demonstrate the use case of applying LLMs to develop such measurements efficiently and at scale.
qs.a: GPTs are GPTs: An Early Look at the Labor Market Impact Potential of Large Language Models · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Large differences in productivity projections depend on adoption, scaling and generalisability assumptions.
kps.d: Acemoglu’s May 2024 calculation implies a cumulative 0.66% US total factor productivity gain over ten years, reduced to an approximately 0.53% upper bound after allowing for hard-to-learn tasks. It assumes 4.6% of tasks become economically affected, extrapolating a computer-vision profitability estimate. Scaling Laws for Economic Productivity challenges both that extrapolation and reliance on older models: its translation experiment finds speed and quality improvements with training compute, then projects 6.95% decade-long productivity growth by assuming transferable relative scaling gains and profitability wherever LLMs improve productivity. Those assumptions are not experimentally established across the economy. Briggs and Kodnani instead project a 1.5-percentage-point annual US labour-productivity growth boost, beginning around half-business adoption, with reemployment and augmentation assumptions. Their eventual 7% global GDP increase is a level effect, not annual growth, and remains outside their baseline forecasts.

qs.q: In other words, according to this basic estimation strategy, TFP gains over the next 10 years from AI are about 0.66%—meaning that relative to the baseline without the current suite of AI and computer vision advances, TFP will be higher by 0.66 percentage points in 10 years, or annual TFP growth will be higher by around 0.064%.
qs.a: The Simple Macroeconomics of AI · Academia · 2024

qs.q: This means that for the purpose of this calculation we assume that if LLMs can increase productivity on a task it will always be profitable.
qs.a: Scaling Laws for Economic Productivity: Experimental Evidence in LLM-Assisted Translation · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Verification and tasks that remain difficult can sharply reduce the value of raw speedups.
kps.d: Anthropic’s January 2026 analysis projects 1.8 percentage points of additional annual labour-productivity growth from Claude usage. Scaling savings by task-success rates reduces this to 1.2 points for Claude.ai and 1.0 for API use; combining reliability adjustments with a complementary-task scenario yields 0.8 and 0.6 points. These are model-based projections, not measured verification costs or realised macroeconomic gains. Claude estimates task durations, and inclusion thresholds materially change results. Acemoglu separately argues that context-dependent work without reliable outcome measures limits extrapolation from easier tasks. Human-AI Productivity Paradoxes offers a theoretical skill–effort explanation for productivity failures that need not disappear after organisational adjustment; its supplied excerpt does not establish economy-wide effects.

qs.q: Additionally adjusting for task success further reduces the implied productivity effects to 0.8pp for [Claude.ai](http://claude.ai/redirect/website.v1.f59e8ddf-c0a1-4146-baf7-80498800ed56) and 0.6pp for API.
qs.a: Anthropic Economic Index Report: Economic Primitives (January 2026) · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: early evidence is from easy-to-learn tasks, whereas some of the future effects will come from hard-to-learn tasks, where there are many context-dependent factors affecting decision-making and no objective outcome measures from which to learn successful performance.
qs.a: The Simple Macroeconomics of AI · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Broad adoption does not establish intensive use or conversion of saved time into additional output.
kps.d: The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI reports that 23% of employed US respondents used generative AI during the working week in 2024, but direct use occupied an estimated 1–5% of total work hours. November respondents reported savings of 5.4% among users and 1.4% across all workers. A wage-weighted model produces a 1.1% potential productivity gain at current usage, conditional on redeploying saved time productively. These are self-reported counterfactual savings, not experimental output measurements. Acemoglu treats organisational adjustment as a constraint; Who is using AI to code? treats integration, training and complementary-asset lags as grounds for longer-run optimism. GPTs are GPTs likewise expects diffusion and complementary technologies to expand effects even without further capability advances.

qs.q: Combining detailed data on the frequency and intensity of genAI usage, we estimate that between 1 and 5 percent of total work hours in the previous week were spent using genAI.
qs.a: The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Historically, early-stage productivity effects of general purpose technologies have been hard to identify because it takes time to integrate them into firm level workflows and procedures, train individuals and amass the complementary assets needed to fully exploit their potential.
qs.a: Who is using AI to code? Global diffusion and impact of generative AI · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Task substitution can coexist with stable employment because reallocation and firm growth offset direct losses.
kps.d: Artificial Intelligence and the Labor Market finds that greater task exposure reduces relative skill demand, while concentrated exposure allows workers to shift effort and adopting firms expand employment. Its estimates concern first-wave AI during 2014–2023 among publicly traded firms, not net generative-AI job losses. Some business, financial and engineering occupations nevertheless lose employment share. The OECD explains why offsets depend on price pass-through, demand elasticity and creation of new tasks. Briggs and Kodnani’s no-displacement scenario still produces substantial productivity gains through augmentation. Thus neither exposure nor productivity growth alone determines labour demand, and stable totals can conceal occupational redistribution.

qs.q: Because the dependent variable is a share, this implies reallocation of labor effort away from exposed tasks and toward less-exposed tasks within the same occupation.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence and the Labor Market · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Finally, the productivity effect depends on the share of the cost savings from AI that are passed along to customers in the form of lower prices and the elasticity of demand for the final product.7 To summarise, there are two key questions concerning the effect of AI on aggregate employment.
qs.a: OECD Employment Outlook 2023: Artificial Intelligence and the Labour Market · Regulators & courts · 2023

kps.k: Larger gains for novices in some tasks do not establish lower wage inequality or stronger entry-level hiring.
kps.d: Generative AI at Work reports 34% more resolutions per hour for the lowest pre-treatment skill quintile, no productivity increase for the most skilled, and no deterioration in its reported service-quality measures. The translation experiment similarly finds larger time reductions among slower baseline performers. These measures of skill differ from education and seniority. The literature review in Does Generative AI Narrow Education-Based Productivity Gaps? reports both novice-favouring experiments and Daniotti et al.’s contrasting finding of gains concentrated among experienced developers. Anthropic also leaves open whether complex-task limitations increase the value of professional expertise. Acemoglu shows theoretically that narrower task-productivity gaps can coexist with greater income inequality; his distributional projections remain especially speculative.

qs.q: In Panel A, we show that the productivity impact of AI assistance is most pronounced for workers in the lowest skill quintile (leftmost side), who see a .29 log point or 34% increase in resolutions per hour.
qs.a: Generative AI at Work · Academia · 2025

qs.q: In particular, whilst high-skilled participants reduce their time taken by 4.9% for every 10x increase in compute those with low- skill have a 21.1% reduction (p=0.017).
qs.a: Scaling Laws for Economic Productivity: Experimental Evidence in LLM-Assisted Translation · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Early macroeconomic and labour-market indicators remain mixed and do not resolve causal attribution.
kps.d: Peter McCrory interprets US output-per-hour growth of 2.0% annually from 2022Q1 to 2026Q1, versus 1.6% in the four pre-pandemic years, as suggestive of AI effects. He acknowledges weaker utilisation-adjusted TFP evidence and reports stable labour-market flows and a relative rebound in software-engineering postings after May 2025. These comparisons do not isolate AI’s causal contribution. The supplied seniority-biased-change review separately reports declining employment for ages 22–25 in highly exposed occupations since late 2022, without a usable magnitude, and Humlum and Vestergaard’s finding of no earnings or hours effects in Denmark despite rapid adoption. Different populations, periods and outcomes prevent treating these claims as direct contradictions.

qs.q: I believe we're starting to see AI's impact in aggregate productivity statistics:  Labor productivity growth has been relatively strong in recent years: the ratio of output per hour of work increased 2.0% per year from 2022Q1 to 2026Q1, as compared to 1.6% in the four years prior to the pandemic.
qs.a: Peter McCrory on X: 'Why hasn't AI increased unemployment?' — Anthropic's head of economics synthesises 18 months of research into a skill-biased, labor-augmenting framework for why AI has produced no material rise in US unemployment · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: (2025a) show that since the late-2022 debut of GenAI, employment of young entry-level workers (ages 22-25) in the most AI-exposed occupations fell by    6 Two related studies examine the effects of Generative AI adoption.
qs.a: Generative AI as Seniority-Biased Technological Change: Evidence from U.S. Résumé and Job Posting Data · Academia · 2025

kps.k: GDP, worker welfare and household value can move differently.
kps.d: Acemoglu argues that investment and potentially harmful AI-created activities can raise measured GDP without equivalent welfare gains. Conversely, the adoption survey notes that workers may take saved time as leisure, improving welfare without increasing output. Google ATLAS models annual US household value just below $60 billion with assumed 2% time savings and about $149 billion at 5%; it does not observe those savings. Its disproportionate legal-help usage indicates demand for assistance, not verified advice quality or resolution of unmet legal need. The coding-diffusion paper’s tens-of-billions social-surplus calculations likewise depend on elasticity scenarios. These valuations are not interchangeable with measured productivity or GDP.

qs.q: In particular, if the capital-output ratio rises and the increase in GDP is more pronounced than that implied by equation (13), then the GDP response would overstate the increase in consumer welfare, as investment comes at the expense of consumption (Acemoglu and Restrepo, 2022).
qs.a: The Simple Macroeconomics of AI · Academia · 2024

qs.q: If workers are now able to complete the same tasks in less time without their employer’s knowledge, they may take their time savings as on-the-job leisure, which would increase welfare but not productivity.
qs.a: The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Practical implications centre on measuring complete workflows, distributional effects and the mechanisms behind aggregate outcomes.
kps.d: The analyses support tracking adoption breadth and intensity alongside quality, verification time, task reallocation, actual output and employment—not treating model capability or usage as realised value. Google and Anthropic associate adoption patterns with income and geography, leaving the direction of international inequality effects unresolved. Google’s exclusion of enterprise-contracted logs also limits conclusions about corporate and agentic workflows. The OECD recommends identifying which employment channels harm which groups; Acemoglu advocates new tasks and stronger worker expertise. These proposals address how benefits might spread rather than assuming that cheaper inference, rapid diffusion or a general-purpose-technology label guarantees broadly shared gains.

qs.q: It will be important to continue tracking the scale, intensity, and heterogeneity of genAI adoption over time.
qs.a: The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Combined with income-driven differences in how AI is used, this raises questions about whether AI will narrow or widen international economic gaps.
qs.a: Anthropic Economic Index Report: Economic Primitives (January 2026) · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

vlens.an:
The selected academia and research sources collectively accept the proposition’s central distinction between task-level AI gains and realised aggregate productivity, employment and welfare, while materially developing the mechanisms that connect them. Their common reasoning is that aggregate outcomes depend on the economic share of affected tasks, profitable and intensive adoption, workflow integration, difficult residual work, complementary assets, task reallocation, firm growth and whether saved time becomes additional output. Several sources also distinguish measured exposure or self-reported savings from realised economic effects.

Material internal variation concerns magnitude, mechanism and evidential status rather than the proposition’s core. Acemoglu projects modest ten-year gains because adoption, organisational adjustment and hard-to-learn tasks constrain scaling; the translation study projects much larger gains by assuming continuing model scaling, transferable relative improvements and profitability wherever LLMs raise productivity. Coding-diffusion and general-purpose-technology accounts are more optimistic about delayed gains from diffusion and complementary technologies, but frame much of that case as expectation rather than demonstrated economy-wide impact. Labour-market research adds that direct task substitution can coexist with muted net employment effects through worker reallocation and adopting-firm growth, subject to limited external validity. Theoretical work further argues that productivity failures may arise from GenAI-specific skill–effort dynamics, not only transitional frictions. Distributional findings are likewise heterogeneous: several studies report larger gains for novices or lower performers, while others find gains concentrated among experienced users; none of this by itself establishes lower inequality or stronger entry-level employment. These sources are a curated selection and should not be treated as representative of academia generally.

qs.q: I show that when AI’s microeconomic effects are driven by cost savings (equiva- lently, productivity improvements) at the task level—due to either automation or task complementarities—its macroeconomic consequences will be given by a version of Hulten’s theorem: GDP and aggregate productivity gains can be estimated by what fraction of tasks are impacted and average task-level cost savings.
qs.a: The Simple Macroeconomics of AI · Academia · 2024

qs.q: By focusing on realized employment changes at the firm–occupation–task level, our analysis helps explain why aggregate effects appear muted even as substitution is evident at the micro level.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence and the Labor Market · Academia · 2025

vlens.an: The selected legal-tech-vendor sources collectively build on the proposition’s core distinction between task-level acceleration and realised aggregate outcomes. Google’s ATLAS contributes usage evidence showing broad but shallow and mainly collaborative adoption, while explicitly declining to infer productivity from interaction logs and making household-value estimates conditional on assumed time savings. Anthropic materially extends the proposition by modelling two mechanisms that cause raw speedups to shrink at scale: imperfect task success, used as a proxy adjustment for reliability and verification, and bottlenecks from complementary residual tasks. Its projections quantify large reductions from those adjustments but remain model-based rather than observed economy-wide gains. Internal variation is substantial: Google is primarily descriptive and cautious about causal or macroeconomic conclusions; Anthropic offers more affirmative numerical projections whose results vary sharply with modelling assumptions; and the methodological excerpt reports research designs without enough findings to take a position. These sources provide limited direct evidence on employment reallocation: Google characterises current use as largely augmentative, while Anthropic leaves displacement, demand and the value of complementary expertise contingent rather than establishing stable employment.

qs.q: First, because ATLAS measures de-identified interactions rather than productivity outcomes, we cannot yet answer how (and if) these micro-level task savings translate into macro-level total factor productivity increases.
qs.a: Google's AI & Economy ATLAS v1.0: Mapping Gemini Usage in the Economy · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

vlens.an: The OECD source builds on the cluster’s principal proposition. It agrees that task-level AI capability or productivity gains do not mechanically determine aggregate employment, then materially extends the analysis by specifying the economic channels that mediate the outcome: price pass-through, demand elasticity, displacement, productivity effects and reinstatement. It also develops the practical implication into a regulatory diagnostic: policymakers should identify which mechanisms dominate and which worker groups bear the harm before choosing interventions. There is some internal variation in emphasis, but not in overall direction. Its capability discussion highlights progress in non-routine cognitive abilities relevant to high-skill occupations, based on evidence as of 2015; this concerns technical capability rather than realised job loss and therefore does not contradict its more conditional labour-market analysis. Because the supplied professional voice contains only this OECD source, the finding characterises that source rather than regulators, courts or professional bodies generally.

qs.q: Finally, the productivity effect depends on the share of the cost savings from AI that are passed along to customers in the form of lower prices and the elasticity of demand for the final product.7 To summarise, there are two key questions concerning the effect of AI on aggregate employment.
qs.a: OECD Employment Outlook 2023: Artificial Intelligence and the Labour Market · Regulators & courts · 2023

qs.q: The effects that are dominating point to which groups’ employment prospects may be most harmed by AI and suggest specific points where policy makers may wish to intervene to ensure that the cost savings from AI do not result in lower demand for labour (see Section 3.3 for a discussion of policies).
qs.a: OECD Employment Outlook 2023: Artificial Intelligence and the Labour Market · Regulators & courts · 2023

vlens.an: The curated market-analyst, consultancy and press sources support the proposition that selected task-level gains do not translate mechanically into aggregate productivity or job losses. Both treat aggregate outcomes as conditional and find that productivity improvement can coexist with stable employment. Briggs and Kodnani provide a forward-looking scenario model in which capability, adoption speed, augmentation, displacement and reemployment produce a wide range of productivity outcomes; their estimates are projections rather than observed effects and are excluded from their baseline forecasts. McCrory instead interprets recent macroeconomic indicators as tentative evidence that gains may already be emerging, while stable labour-market flows suggest no unusual aggregate disruption. Material internal variation therefore concerns evidence and timing: Briggs and Kodnani model potentially large future gains under explicit assumptions, whereas McCrory draws a cautious inference from current correlations and acknowledges that weaker total factor productivity evidence limits causal attribution. Neither directly examines verification costs or complete-workflow scaling, so their support is strongest for the proposition’s adoption, reallocation and employment components. These sources are a curated selection and should not be treated as representative of all market analysts, consultancies or press commentary.

qs.q: But across quits, layoffs, and job finding rates, we see a pattern of stability.
qs.a: Peter McCrory on X: 'Why hasn't AI increased unemployment?' — Anthropic's head of economics synthesises 18 months of research into a skill-biased, labor-augmenting framework for why AI has produced no material rise in US unemployment · Market & press · 2026

elens.an: The 2015–2022 source accepts and materially develops the proposition’s task-based account of aggregate productivity and employment. Rather than treating automation as a direct proxy for labour displacement, it supplies an estimation framework that separates capital–labour substitution from changes in the task content of production and, with further assumptions, distinguishes displacement from labour reinstatement through new tasks. This strengthens the proposition’s claim that reallocation and new work can offset direct task losses and that aggregate outcomes depend on mechanisms beyond task-level speedups. The source does not address later generative-AI issues such as adoption intensity, verification, difficult residual tasks or AI-specific productivity projections. Its main internal qualification is methodological: the decomposition depends on competitive-market assumptions, an industry-level substitution elasticity and an additional assumption that industries do not automate while simultaneously introducing new tasks. Thus it builds on the proposition through a concrete analytical method, while leaving important AI-era scaling mechanisms outside its scope.

qs.q: We estimate industry-level change in task content as the residual change in labor share (observed directly in the data) which cannot be explained by the substitution effect.
qs.a: Automation and New Tasks: How Technology Displaces and Reinstates Labor · Academia · 2019

qs.q: Under additional assumptions, we can also separate the change in task content into its two components: the displacement and reinstatement effects.
qs.a: Automation and New Tasks: How Technology Displaces and Reinstates Labor · Academia · 2019

elens.an: The curated 2023–2024 sources support the proposition that selected-task speedups do not translate mechanically into aggregate productivity, employment or welfare. Their common reasoning is that macroeconomic effects depend on the economic share of affected tasks and on mediating conditions including profitable adoption, diffusion speed, task difficulty, complementary technologies, demand responses, augmentation, displacement and worker reallocation. Material variation lies chiefly in projected magnitude rather than in this framework: Acemoglu estimates modest ten-year gains after accounting for limited profitable use and hard-to-learn tasks; Briggs and Kodnani project substantially larger but explicitly conditional gains supported by augmentation and reemployment; and the translation-scaling study reaches an even higher estimate by assuming continued model scaling, transferable relative gains and profitability wherever LLMs improve productivity. The OECD develops the employment side by specifying price pass-through, demand elasticity, displacement and reinstatement as causal channels, while GPTs are GPTs confines its empirical contribution to exposure potential and treats broader effects as dependent on diffusion and complementary technologies. Verification is not directly analysed by these sources, but difficult residual tasks and organisational adjustment provide closely related reasons why raw task gains may shrink during scaling.

qs.q: I show that when AI’s microeconomic effects are driven by cost savings (equiva- lently, productivity improvements) at the task level—due to either automation or task complementarities—its macroeconomic consequences will be given by a version of Hulten’s theorem: GDP and aggregate productivity gains can be estimated by what fraction of tasks are impacted and average task-level cost savings.
qs.a: The Simple Macroeconomics of AI · Academia · 2024

elens.an: The curated 2025 sources support the cluster’s principal proposition that selected-task speedups and broad adoption do not translate mechanically into aggregate productivity or employment effects. Their common reasoning is that realised outcomes depend on intervening mechanisms: whether saved time is converted into additional output, how workers reallocate effort across tasks, whether adopting firms expand, and how effects differ by skill and occupation. Material variation concerns what each source can establish. The first-wave 2014–2023 firm evidence directly identifies task substitution alongside offsetting reallocation and firm growth, but cautions against generalising its magnitudes to generative AI. The 2024 adoption survey finds widespread but low-intensity use and derives only a conditional potential productivity gain from self-reported time savings. Customer-support evidence establishes substantial gains for lower-skilled workers without supporting broader conclusions about wages, hiring or aggregate productivity. The seniority-focused review adds uneven labour-market evidence—entry-level weakness in highly exposed US occupations but no measured earnings or hours effects in Denmark. Collectively, these sources reinforce rather than extend the synthesis: they substantiate scaling and reallocation constraints, while offering little direct evidence on verification costs or difficult residual tasks.

qs.q: By focusing on realized employment changes at the firm–occupation–task level, our analysis helps explain why aggregate effects appear muted even as substitution is evident at the micro level.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence and the Labor Market · Academia · 2025

qs.q: However, labor productivity gains will only translate into aggregate productivity gains if firms adjust their expectations.
qs.a: The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI · Academia · 2025

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources collectively accept the proposition’s central distinction between task-level acceleration and realised aggregate productivity, while materially developing the mechanisms that govern scaling. Anthropic quantifies how reliability adjustments and complementary-task bottlenecks reduce projected gains; Human-AI Productivity Paradoxes adds a theoretical skill–effort mechanism under which productivity failures may persist beyond transitional organisational frictions. Google ATLAS reinforces the measurement distinction by showing broad but shallow, mainly collaborative use while explicitly declining to infer macro productivity from interaction logs. Common reasons include incomplete workflow integration, uneven adoption, verification or reliability constraints, difficult residual tasks, and uncertainty over whether saved time becomes additional output. Material internal variation concerns optimism and evidentiary strength: the coding-diffusion study expects substantial longer-run gains after complementary investment, while McCrory reads recent labour-productivity growth as an emerging but non-causal signal; ATLAS and Anthropic rely on usage data and model-based projections rather than realised economy-wide outcomes. The reviewed distributional evidence also varies by setting, with some studies favouring novices and others experienced developers. One methods-only excerpt reports research designs without findings and is therefore unclear rather than affirmative. None of this establishes a general 2026 employment effect: McCrory reports stable aggregate labour-market flows, while theoretical and projection-based sources leave wages, employment and reallocation contingent. This assessment characterises only the supplied curated sources, not all work published in 2026.
